asgardian_tissue_density_ohotmu.notes: Exact OCR snippets from archive.org full-text search; these are lending-library scans, so only about 100 characters around each hit can be seen. Essential OHOTMU Deluxe vol 1 (2006): 'immortal like the Olympian gods), aging at an extraordinarily slow. rate upon reaching adult- hood. Asgardian flesh and bone is about three times denser than similar human...'. Same volume: 'times denser than similar human tissue, contributing to the gods' superhuman Strength and weight. An male'. Other entries in the same volume: '(Asgardian flesh and bone is about three times denser than similar human tissue, contributing to the Asgar- dians' superhuman strength and weight.) His Asgardian metabolism gives him super- human endurance', and 'injury (Asgardian flesh and bone is about 3 times denser than Earthly flesh and bone, accounting for Asgardians'...'. The 1987 vol 4 reads: 'and bone is about 3 times denser than similar human tissue, contributing to the Asgardians superhuman strength and weight.)'. The Definitive Thor Reloaded (2013): 'flesh, bone, and muscle possess about three times the density of the tissue of a human body.' The same 2006 volume's Asgard entry says 'common matter is considerably denser on an average. Con- sequently a chair made of Asgardian...' and 'water, flesh, bone, steel - all mat- . ter is denser and thus more durable'. Wording varies between 'three times denser' and '3 times as dense', so read it as a factor of about 3, not 4. Not confirmed: the issue number and page of each entry. The group entry sits in the part reprinting Deluxe #1-7, probably #1 (the A entries), unverified. No handbook gives a density in kg/m3. The fan wiki cites Thor & Hercules: Encyclopaedia Mythologica (2009) for 'skin, muscle, and bone tissues ... about three times as dense'; I did not fetch that book, so status reported. The fan-wiki infobox also gives an Asgardian 'AvgWeight 450 lbs', uncited (reported). Archive.org also holds unauthorised digital comic uploads that repeat this wording; I deliberately did not cite them.

verify.issue: I re-fetched these on 2026-10-11 and they match. Essential OHOTMU Deluxe vol 1 (officialhandbook0001unse) gives 'Asgardian flesh and bone is about three times denser than similar...', '...times denser than similar human tissue, contributing to the gods' superhuman Strength and weight. An male' and 'flesh and bone is about 3 times denser than Earthly flesh and bone, accounting for Asgardians' greater'. The 1987 TPB vol 4 (officialhandbook04grue) has 'Asgardian flesh and bone is about 3 times denser than similar human tissue, contributing to the Asgardians...'. The Definitive Thor (Panini 2011, ISBN 9781846534812) has the same wording. The Definitive Thor Reloaded (Panini 2013, ISBN 9781846535529) has 'flesh, bone, and muscle possess about three times the density of the tissue of a human body'. All the ISBNs and dates agree with the archive.org metadata. A small point: OHOTMU itself always says 'times denser'. The 'as dense' and 'the density' wording comes from DK and Reloaded, not from the handbook. A caveat to add: the 2004 handbook 'Avengers part one' (archive.org officialhandbook0000unse_z5q7, which is full-text searchable) says Thor 'possesses the superhuman physical attributes of an Asgardian god, but to a much greater degree'. So applying the generic Asgardian factor to Thor is itself an assumption. The same 2004 book says of Hercules: 'His flesh and bones are several times denser than a human's'. Handbook density factors are loose. Citation problem: the archive.org full-text search URLs often fail. About half of them returned HTTP 400 with 'FTS API ... HTTP 502' on my first tries; the all-texts query only worked when shortened to '"denser than similar human"'. Cite the item pages as well.

thor_density_adjusted_mass.label: Thor: official weight converted to human-tissue-equivalent mass (official weight divided by 3)

sources.title: Marvel.com Thor (Thor Odinson) In Comics (640 lb, 6 ft 6 in)

Archive.org full-text search, Essential OHOTMU Deluxe vol 1: 'denser than similar human tissue' [archive.org search API: it often fails, so retry later; it matched “…flesh and bone is about three times denser than similar human tissue, contributing to the Asgar- dians’…”]

The official handbook of the Marvel universe. Vol. 1 (2006), archive.org (lending library: borrow it to read the page): “…flesh and bone is about three times denser than similar human tissue, contributing to the Asgar- dians’…”

thor_density_adjusted_mass.notes: Method: a body of the same size and shape made of ordinary tissue would weigh the listed mass divided by the density ratio: 290.3 / 3 = 96.8 kg (213 lb). S = 1.8 x FFM / H^3 and FFMI = FFM / H^2 at assumed fat of 0, 10 and 15% (body fat is unknown). Assumes all tissue is 3x as dense, following OHOTMU's 'flesh and bone'. If only skin and bone are denser (DK's wording), the correction is smaller. I have not computed that case, because it needs tissue mass fractions not researched here. A numerical observation only, which Marvel does not state: 213 lb is close to Donald Blake's 150 lb scaled isometrically to 6 ft 6 in (217 lb, existing key plausibility_metrics). Relies on existing builds.json keys thor (height and weight) and plausibility_metrics. Rounded to what the inputs support: 'about three times' carries perhaps one significant figure, so the 97 kg value is about plus or minus a third.

verify.issue: I recomputed every number. 640 lb = 290.3 kg, and /3 = 96.77 kg (213.3 lb). The S values are 67.19/60.47/57.12 (listed) and 22.40/20.16/19.04 (adjusted). Plain FFMI is 24.65/22.19. Blake scaled isometrically comes out at 216.7 lb. All match. Two problems with how it is presented. (1) The 'about plus or minus a third' uncertainty is not carried into the S values. With a factor of 2-4, or 97 kg plus or minus a third, S at 10% fat runs from about 13-15 to about 27-30, not '20-22'. (2) S of 20-22 is below the brief's US Army median (about 24). The number is the handbook's round-number arithmetic, not a description of the heavily muscled figure Marvel draws. It must not be presented as Thor's muscle level.
verify.corrected: Show S_equiv as a range: about 15-30 at 10% fat for a density factor of 2-4. Label it 'what the handbook's density figure implies, derived', not 'Thor's build'.

thing_rocky_hide.notes:
Marvel.com: 'his rock-like skin has only been known to be pierced by extraterrestrial weaponry or sorcerous means, and while uncomfortable-looking is actually supple and allows him a wealth of movement.' Also: 'Grimm's outward form mutates over his years as the Thing, changing from a lumpy hide to what appears to be individual rocks linked together'. The Marvel.com guide: 'From his original human form to his rocky exterior and beyond'. DK 2019: 'Ben's skin turned orange and rocky, and his strength grew'; powers 'Superhuman strength, endurance, and durability. He can lift 85 tons'. Official wording therefore names the skin, hide or exterior. Fan wiki (reported; these sentences cite no source): 'Body is covered with an orange, flexible, rock-like hide'; 'The mutagenic process caused his overall musculature, bone structure, internal organ composition, soft tissue structure, and skin to also greatly increase in toughness and density'; 'The rock-like composition of the Thing's body renders him highly resistant to physical injury.' I could not reach the OHOTMU Thing entry text: the Deluxe Thing entry is not in the searchable volumes, and full-text search for 'rocklike hide' found only Sanderson's Marvel Universe (1998), 'enormous strength and a nearly impenetrable, rocklike hide'. No source gives the hide's thickness, density or mass. Listed weight and height come from the existing key thing.

Correction (verifier): Label: 'The Thing: official sources describe rock-like, supple skin or hide; they say nothing about what is under it or how much it weighs.' Notes: the fan wiki's density sentence is in a paragraph that cites The Thing Vol 3 #1 (2022, not seen); status reported.

verify.issue: The quotes and numbers check out. Marvel.com: 'rock-like skin ... supple', 'lumpy hide to what appears to be individual rocks linked together', 'HEIGHT 6' WEIGHT 500 lbs.' The Marvel.com guide: 'rocky exterior'. DK 2019: 'Ben's skin turned orange and rocky' and 'He can lft 85 tons'. S = 66.74/60.07/56.73. The label goes beyond the sources, though. 'Not a body of rock' is the researcher's inference: no official text says what lies under the skin, and Marvel.com's 'individual rocks linked together' cuts the other way. One note is also slightly wrong. On the fan wiki, the 'toughness and density' sentence sits in a paragraph that ends with {{r|Thing Vol 3 1}}, so it is not clearly uncited. The 'rock-like composition' line has no citation. Still reported, because the comic was not seen.

comic_score_treatment.notes:
These are my recommendations, built on the facts above; they are not official.
- Comparable means the listed mass is described as ordinary tissue, or nothing official says otherwise.
- Overstated means official text says part of the mass is not ordinary tissue, or the tissue is denser, so the score built from listed mass is too high. A factor is given only where a source gives a figure.
- Not comparable means the body is not tissue at all.
By character:
- Thor and Asgardians: divide by about 3.
- Wolverine: subtract the official 105 lb.
- Colossus, armoured: steel-like body.
- The Thing and Luke Cage: overstated by an unknown amount.
- Hulk and Abomination: the handbook calls the added mass bone marrow and (muscle) tissue.
- Juggernaut: no source says whether the 900 lb includes his helmet and armour.
- Darkseid and Doomsday: comparable only because nothing official says otherwise.
- Superman, Batman, Captain America and Black Panther: human-plausible, and no official density statement exists.

nhanes_dxa_bodyfat_men_1999_2004.notes: Table 3, 'Total percentage body fat ... Male, All race and ethnicity': 'Age 20 years and older, crude ... 6,559 28.0 0.1 17.4 19.5 21.4 24.1 28.0 32.1 34.3 35.9 38.0'; '20-39 years ... 2,183 26.1 0.1 15.5 17.4 18.9 21.2 26.1 30.4 32.8 34.6 37.2'. Methods: people over 300 lb or taller than 6'5" were not scanned ('physical limitations of the DXA table'). Missing or invalid scans were multiply imputed. 'Participant lean mass was decreased by 5% and an equivalent kilogram weight added to the fat mass', because the QDR 4500A was shown to underestimate fat (Schoeller et al.). The published %fat therefore already includes that correction. Weighted, nationally representative. Best primary source for 'everyday men'. Kelly, Wilson & Heymsfield 2009 (PLoS ONE, PMC2737140) uses the same NHANES DXA data. I fetched it, but its percentiles are in supplementary LMS files, so I used the NCHS tables instead.

values.method: 3-site skinfold, Evans et al. 2005 athlete equation (4C-derived)

sources.title: Rosaci G, Biban S, Bartolomei S. Beyond the Limits of Human Muscle Hypertrophy: A Case Study of a Mr. Olympia Competitor Bodybuilder. J Strength Cond Res 2026;40(10):1253-1258, Table 3 and methods (Europe PMC full text PMC13592830)

Drug status: 'The eventual use of performance enhancing drugs by the athlete, competing in IFBB Pro League contests, in which antidoping tests are not performed, was not considered'. Equation: '% body fat = 8.997 + 0.24658 x (SUM 3 SKF) - 6.343 x (sex) - 1.998 x (race)'. For a white man it cannot go below 2.65% even at zero skinfold. A 6.1% off-season reading at 128.7 kg is implausibly low for this method and probably an underestimate. I treat the FFM, and so the FFMI of about 37-39, as upper bounds. Single subject. Best published body composition of a current top-level (presumably enhanced) pro that I found. The authors also cite Moreno et al. 2024 (Am J Hum Biol, PMID 37563889) for an Open bodybuilder of 131.4 kg at 12.2% fat. I fetched only Moreno's abstract, which gives ultrasound-estimated skeletal muscle (60.4 kg at most) and neither number, so the 12.2% is second-hand.

The average maximal contact forces for each leg were 34.2% bodyweight during squatting and 30.9% bodyweight during kneeling. Corresponding average maximal knee flexion angles were 151.8 degrees during squatting and 156.4 degrees during kneeling. Thigh and calf circumferences were correlated with the contact force measurements.' Zelle 2009: 'there was a clear correlation between a subject's thigh and calf circumference and the force reduction at maximal flexion due to thigh-calf contact (R=0.89)'. Hemmerich 2006 (30 Indian adults): 'A mean maximum flexion of 157 degrees +/- 6 degrees at the knee joint was required for squatting with heels up.' Useful as a compression allowance: under about a third of body weight, soft tissue lets the knee bend some 20-25° past first contact. This is the only quantitative contact-onset vs end-of-range data found; it is for the knee, not the elbow.

verify.issue: All three abstracts are verbatim: no contact below 130°, 34.2%/30.9% BW, 151.8°/156.4°, R=0.89, Hemmerich 157±6. Two cautions. (1) Girth is correlated with contact force and force reduction, not with the angle at which contact starts, so 'contact scales with girth' should not be read as 'onset angle falls with girth'. (2) 'The knee bends 20-25° past first contact' is the researcher's own derivation. Onset is only bounded ('not below 130°'), so 22-26° is an upper bound; mark it derived.

hip_joint_centre_regression_hara2016.label: Hip joint centre lateral offset = 8 mm + 0.086 x leg length (Hara et al. 2016, imaging-based regression)

values.leg_length_definition: ASIS to medial malleolus through the medial femoral epicondyle

sources.title: Hara R, McGinley J, Briggs C, Baker R, Sangeux M. Predicting the location of the hip joint centres, impact of age group and sex. Sci Rep 2016;6:37707, doi 10.1038/srep37707 (PMC page)
Same article, PMC full-text XML via NCBI E-utilities

Bell AL, Pedersen DR, Brand RA. A comparison of the accuracy of several hip center location prediction methods. J Biomech 1990;23:617-621 (record only, no abstract)

hip_joint_centre_regression_hara2016.notes:
Hara et al.: 'We propose the equations with leg length as single predictor'; read via the PMC page: HJC_X = 11 - 0.063 LL, HJC_Y (medial-lateral) = 8 + 0.086 LL, HJC_Z = -9 - 0.078 LL (mm; units implied by mm errors). Leg length = 'Distance from ASIS to medial malleolus through the medial epicondyle of the femur'. 'Using leg length as the single predictor, the accuracy of the regression equations to locate the HJC was 5.2 mm, 4.4 mm, and 3.8 mm in the posterior-anterior, medial-lateral and inferior-superior directions'; 'our analysis did not support the use of additional ... (age, sex) predictors'. The formulas are images in the XML, so I read them through the rendered page. Harrington 2007 (8 adults, MRI) found pelvic width and depth best for the medial-lateral direction. Its exact equation (reported second-hand as ML = 0.33 x inter-ASIS + 7.3 mm) was NOT verified in the primary source. Used to fix the leg axes for the thigh-contact test.

Also researched under the outline topic (measured): Hara 2016: CT of 157 deceased individuals (37 children, 120 skeletally mature). HJC = centre of the femoral head. Table 2 and the text: "HJC X = 11 −0.063 LL, HJC Y = 8 +0.086 LL, and HJC Z = −9 −0.078 LL", where LL is clinical leg length, ASIS to medial malleolus through the medial femoral epicondyle, and IA is the inter-ASIS distance. Accuracy: "5.2 mm, 4.4 mm, and 3.8 mm in the posterior-anterior, medial-lateral and inferior-superior directions". Table 3 gives Bell et al.'s equations applied to the Hara data: 8.1, 6.1, 10.9 mm.

Harrington 2007 abstract: "Maximum absolute errors of 31 mm were found in adults" for three common regression equations. Its own equations are not quoted in the abstract.

Bell 1990 and Harrington full texts are paywalled, so Bell's coefficients are not verified here. All of these work from bony pelvic landmarks (ASIS), which ANSUR II does not measure. For a silhouette, use the trochanter-level rule plus the inter-HJC estimate.

verify.issue: Confirmed in the PMC XML (Table 3 footnote, as text): 'HJCX = 11 −0.063 LL, HJCY = 8 +0.086 LL, and HJCZ = −9 −0.078 LL'. Accuracy is 5.2/4.4/3.8 mm. The origin is the mid-point between the ASIS, with HJC 'lateral' to it, so Y is the offset from the midline and the inter-HJC = 2Y use is right. Two corrections to the notes. The formulas are not only images; they are in the table footnote text. The sample, which the notes omit, is cadaveric CT of '157 deceased individuals (37 children, 120 skeletally matured)'. 'Measured' is acceptable for a published regression, though 'derived' would be more exact.
verify.corrected: notes: add sample = CT scans of 157 deceased individuals (120 skeletally mature)

ansur_thigh_gap_legs_vertical.label: Gap between the thighs just above the knee with legs vertical: ANSUR II men (estimate from girths and a hip-joint regression)

sources.title: ANSUR II male CSV (OPEN Design Lab), same file as build-calculator/data/ansur2/ANSUR_II_MALE_Public.csv
Hara et al. 2016 Sci Rep 6:37707 (hip joint centre regression)

ansur_thigh_gap_legs_vertical.notes: Script: scratchpad/research/functional-limits/scripts/ansur_thighgap.py. Per man: leg length LL is estimated as iliocristale height - 0.06 m - (lateral malleolus height + 0.01 m), an assumption because ANSUR II has no ASIS height. HJC offset = 8 + 0.086 LL (mm). Legs vertical means ankle centres directly under the hip joint centres (0° hip abduction). Lower-thigh half-width = ANSUR lower thigh circumference (suprapatellar site) / 2π, assuming a circular cross-section centred on the leg axis. Result: the median man has about 4.4 cm between his thighs just above the knee; only 1 of 4,082 men has zero gap; the median man's lower-thigh width must grow about 1.34x about the leg axis to close it. For comparison, with ankle centres one biacromial breadth apart ('feet shoulder-width'), the factor is about 2.2. With heels together (ANSUR standing), most men's knees nearly meet, so the stance choice moves this limit by a large amount. Ignores: non-circular thighs, medial bulk (vastus medialis, adductors) off the axis, compression, knee valgus or varus. Relies on existing builds.json keys ansur2_dataset and ansur2_thigh.

verify.issue: Re-running ansur_thighgap.py on the local CSV (sha256 identical to the OPEN Design Lab download) reproduces every number. Inter-HJC 0.160/0.174/0.189, gap 0.024/0.044/0.063 m, one man at zero, k 1.17/1.34/1.53, feet shoulder-width 2.17. Not tested: sensitivity to the leg-length estimate (iliocristale −6 cm). A ±5 cm leg-length error moves Y by ±4.3 mm and the gap by about ±0.9 cm. Note too that ANSUR soldiers meet Army weight standards, so the very obese, who likely do close this gap, are under-represented.

ansur_seated_arm_angle.label: How far ANSUR II men's upper arms angle out when hanging at the sides (seated, elbows 90 deg), from forearm-forearm breadth (estimate)

sources.title: ANSUR II male CSV (OPEN Design Lab)
ANSUR II Measurer's Handbook, sec. 6.1.2 sitting posture and 6.4.40 forearm-forearm breadth

ansur_seated_arm_angle.notes: Script: scratchpad/research/functional-limits/scripts/ansur_armangle.py. Posture: 'the upper arms are hanging loosely at the sides ... flex the elbows 90° ... palms facing inward'. Forearm-forearm breadth is the maximum distance across the outsides of the forearms. Angle = asin((FFB/2 - flexed forearm girth/2π - (biacromial/2 - 0.02)) / (acromion-radiale - 0.03)). The shoulder-joint offset (0.015-0.03 m tried) and upper-arm length are assumptions. Result: men's hanging arms angle out about 10° (median), 19° at the 99th percentile and 26° at most (a short man, BMI 35.5). The angle rises with BMI (r 0.69). The highest values belong to high-BMI men, not to the men with the biggest arms. A rough but data-based spread of the human range for the arm-hang limit; seated, not standing.

verify.issue: ansur_armangle.py reproduces every number: p5/p50/p95/p99/max 3.6/10.0/16.5/19.2/26.2; offset range 9.0-11.9 and 25.1-28.5; r 0.69 and 0.57; BMI medians 6.4/9.9/13.2/15.5. Two cautions. It is a seated angle that runs about 4-6° above the standing model's 4-6° at k=1, so the two scales are not interchangeable. And ANSUR excludes very obese men, so 'max 26°' describes screened soldiers, not all humans.

arm_hang_model_ansur_median.label: Front-view arm rest angle vs width factor, ANSUR II median man (simple 2D model, estimate)

sources.title: ANSUR II male CSV (OPEN Design Lab)

arm_hang_model_ansur_median.notes:
Script: scratchpad/research/functional-limits/scripts/arm_hang.py. Uses ANSUR medians: shoulder joint 2 cm medial and 4 cm below the acromion (estimate); torso half-widths from chest, waist and hip breadth at their landmark heights; arm half-widths from flexed biceps x 0.93, flexed forearm and wrist girths over 2π. The arm is straight and rotates about the fixed shoulder joint. Widths scale by k about each segment's own axis; the skeleton stays fixed. At k=1 the arm rests 4-6° out, matching ANSUR's 'elbows lightly touching the sides', which checks the model. Testing from the armpit itself is meaningless: arm and torso are joined there by the axillary folds, and the contact would force about 10° even at k=1, so the test region must start below the folds. The choice of test region moves the 30° crossing between k = 1.3 and 1.65. The torso scaled about the midline overstates torso growth (the ribcage does not grow), so real muscular builds with small waists reach the limit later through the waist and sooner through the lats.

hand_to_mouth_reach_geometry.label: Elbow flexion needed for the hand to touch the mouth, from arm and head geometry (ANSUR II median proportions, estimate)

sources.title: ANSUR II male CSV (OPEN Design Lab)
38 CFR 4.71 Plate I (wrist palmar flexion 80 deg)

hand_to_mouth_reach_geometry.notes:
Script: scratchpad/research/functional-limits/scripts/reach.py. With the shoulder free, a hand point can touch the mouth only if its distance from the shoulder joint can equal the shoulder-to-mouth distance. Elbow flexion sets the closest the hand can come, so the needed flexion is where that closest distance equals the mouth distance. Inputs (ANSUR medians, with estimates): shoulder joint to elbow axis 0.31 m (acromion-radiale 0.335 minus offsets), elbow to wrist 0.265 m, hand 0.193 m. Mouth relative to shoulder joint: 0.19 m medial, 0.17 m up, 0.11 m forward (from stature, tragion-to-top-of-head and menton-sellion length; estimate). Straight wrist: about 123° (chin 127°), close to the ~130° the daily-task studies measured for eating and drinking (Morrey, Safaee-Rad), which supports the geometry. Wrist flexed to its 80° limit (38 CFR): about 99° for the mouth, 91-107° across the face. The planar model ignores neck movement, shoulder-girdle movement, and bulk on the chest and deltoid that can block the arm from crossing in front of the body.

elbow_flexion_vs_girth_wedge_model.label: Maximum elbow flexion vs arm girth: a wedge contact model; pure geometry (exponent 1) and a fit to BMI groups (about 1.7) bracket it; neither tested above ordinary girths (estimate)

values.model: tan((180-phi_max)/2) = c * k^p; k = (flexed biceps + flexed forearm girth) / 0.614 m

sources.title: Zwerus et al. 2019 Shoulder Elbow (flexion by BMI group, men)
ANSUR II male CSV (girths by BMI group)

elbow_flexion_vs_girth_wedge_model.notes:
Scripts: scratchpad/research/functional-limits/scripts/elbow_fit.py and ansur_limits.py. Model: the upper arm and forearm close like a wedge until their front tissue fills it. If tissue thickness grows by k at a fixed contact distance, tan(half the remaining angle) grows by k (p=1). c is set so k=1 gives 145° (Zwerus normal-BMI men, active; CDC men 20-44 passive 144.6°; 38 CFR 145°). Check against data: ANSUR II median flexed biceps + forearm girth by BMI group is 555, 614, 666 and 718 mm (k = 0.90, 1, 1.085, 1.17). Zwerus's 151/145/140/136° then implies p = 1.6-2.0, a steeper loss than pure geometry. But p≈1.7 would put elite bodybuilder arms (girth about 1.7x the reference, e.g. a reported 0.61 m flexed arm) near 100°, far below the ~130° the Islam review states for bodybuilders. p=1 gives about 122-129° there. Possible reasons: much of a bodybuilder's arm girth is triceps behind the elbow, which does not block flexion; the BMI groups differ in age and fat; and mapping Dutch BMI groups onto ANSUR girths is approximate. Recommend p=1 as the main model with p≈1.7 as the pessimistic bound. Nothing measured above about k=1.2, so every value beyond is an extrapolation.

Correction (verifier): Present both as a band: p=1 'pure geometry, assumption'; p≈1.7 'fitted to BMI groups (mostly fat, age-confounded)'; neither tested above k≈1.17. Do not call either the main model on the strength of the review statement.

Active p=1.69, passive 1.86. Crossings: 130° at 1.26-1.48, 120° at 1.43-1.83, 110° at 1.60-2.22, 100° at 1.79-2.66. The tan(half-angle) ∝ thickness geometry is right for contact at a fixed axial distance. The problem is the recommendation to make p=1 the 'main model' and the data-fitted p≈1.7 a 'pessimistic bound'. That reverses the evidence. The only measurements (Zwerus BMI groups mapped to ANSUR girths) give p≈1.6-2.0. The case for p=1 rests on the unsourced Bentham-review '130° for bodybuilders' and on a plausible but untested triceps argument. The two exponents put the 100° crossing at S≈65 versus S≈144 on the chart (see rec_rough_order), so this choice decides where limit (c) falls.

soft_tissue_contact_models_survey.label: No published model found that predicts maximum joint flexion from limb girth or cross-section; the nearest are contact-force models and animation tissue simulation

sources.title: McAdams A et al. Efficient elasticity for character skinning with contact and collisions. ACM SIGGRAPH 2011 / ACM TOG 30(4)
Reed MP et al. Developing and implementing parametric human body shape models in ergonomics software (Jack)
Wu JZ et al. Biomechanical modeling of deep squatting: effects of the interface contact between posterior thigh and shank. J Biomech 2019;96:109333, PMID 31558308 (abstract via NCBI E-utilities)
Singh B et al. Abdomen-thigh contact during forward reaching tasks in obese individuals. J Appl Biomech 2013;29(5):517-24, PMID 23183157 (abstract via NCBI E-utilities)

soft_tissue_contact_models_survey.notes: McAdams 2011: 'a new algorithm for near-interactive simulation of skeleton driven, high resolution elasticity models ... Since body collisions, self collisions and soft-constraints are necessary for real-world examples, we present a simple framework for enforcing them.' Joint angles are inputs; tissue deforms to avoid passing through itself; the model does not output a range limit. Reed 2014 (Jack): figures 'can be scaled by inputting standard anthropometric dimensions ... However, the shapes of these scaled figures are often unrealistic, particularly for extreme body types'. The paper covers body shape, not joint range. Wu 2019 (AnyBody): 'in a deep squatting posture (knee flexion 120+ degrees), the posterior thigh/shank contact helps reduce the patellofemoral (PF) and tibiofemoral (TF) normal contact forces by 42% and 57%'. Singh 2013: 'This soft tissue apposition acts as a mechanical restriction'; mean contact force '10.17 ± 5.18% of body weight'. I found no RAMSIS or Jack documentation computing range limits from soft-tissue collision, and no paper predicting elbow flexion from arm cross-section. The wedge model in this set is our own derivation.

ffmi_definition_vanitallie1990.label: FFMI definition: fat-free mass over height squared (VanItallie et al. 1990)

sources.title: VanItallie TB, Yang MU, Heymsfield SB, Funk RC, Boileau RA. Height-normalized indices of the body's fat-free mass and fat mass: potentially useful indicators of nutritional status. Am J Clin Nutr 1990;52:953-959. doi:10.1093/ajcn/52.6.953 (Europe PMC abstract record, PMID 2239792)

ffmi_definition_vanitallie1990.notes: Abstract, verbatim: 'we propose use of height-normalized indices, namely, a FFM index [FFM (kg)/height (m)2, or FFMI] and a BFM index [BFM (kg)/height (m)2, or BFMI]. We calculated these indices in a reference population of 124 healthy young men and in 32 nonobese young men (from the Minnesota Study)'. The stated purpose is clinical: telling malnourished tall patients from well-nourished short ones. The abstract gives no reason for choosing height^2 over another power. The full text (OUP/Elsevier) was not reachable; only the abstract was read. Heymsfield 2007 later wrote that its results 'provide support for the suggestion of Van Itallie et al to normalize fat and FFM for height 2' (see heymsfield2007_ffm_height_power_fulltext). Existing builds.json key ffmi_definition_kouri_limit already has FFMI = FFM/H^2 from Kouri; this adds the original source.

verify.issue: Re-fetched the Europe PMC record for PMID 2239792. The quote is verbatim, and 124 reference men, 32 Minnesota men and '27 of the 32' all match. The abstract gives no reason for choosing height squared, as the researcher says. 'reported' is the right status for a definition.

kouri1995_normalisation_reference.label: Kouri 1995 normalises FFMI to the height of a 1.80 m man (formula as printed in the abstract)

sources.title: Kouri EM, Pope HG, Katz DL, Oliva P. Fat-free mass index in users and nonusers of anabolic-androgenic steroids. Clin J Sport Med 1995;5:223-228 (Europe PMC abstract record, PMID 7496846), re-fetched 2026-10-11

kouri1995_normalisation_reference.notes: Abstract, verbatim: 'FFMI is defined by the formula (fat-free body mass in kg) x (height in meters)-2. We then added a slight correction of 6.3 x (1.80 m - height) to normalize these values to the height of a 1.8-m man.' This relies on and agrees with existing keys kouri1995_normalization_constant and ffmi_height_correction (status disputed: the abstract prints 6.3, while Trexler 2017 and most calculators use 6.1; at most 0.05 FFMI units apart between 1.55 and 2.05 m). The full text is not open access (Europe PMC: no PDF, not OA), so the athletes' height range and how the slope was fitted are unknown. The 1.80 m reference height is the reason the rescaled index uses the constant 1.8: at 1.80 m it then equals both plain and Kouri-normalised FFMI.

verify.issue: Re-fetched PMID 7496846. The abstract prints '6.3 x (1.80 m - height) to normalize these values to the height of a 1.8-m man', with 157 athletes (83 users, 74 nonusers). Europe PMC flags it as not open access. The fact rightly relies on the existing disputed keys for 6.3 vs 6.1. The gap is 0.2 x |1.8 - H|, at most 0.05 between 1.55 and 2.05 m.

geometric_similarity_mass_cubed.label: At the same shape and density, mass (and muscle mass) scales with height cubed and areas with height squared

sources.title: Burton RF. Human allometry: adult bodies are more nearly geometrically similar than regression analysis has suggested. Med Hypotheses 2010;74:15-17 (Europe PMC abstract, PMID 19726135)

Burton R. The Sitting-Height Index of Build, (Body Mass)/(Sitting Height)^3, as an Improvement on the Body Mass Index for Children, Adolescents and Young Adults. Children (Basel) 2018;5(2):30 (PMC full text, CC BY)
Haldane JBS. On Being the Right Size (transcription from 'On Being the Right Size and Other Essays', OUP 1985; marxists.org)
Harper's Magazine archive page: 'On being the right size', J.B.S. Haldane, March 1926 (publication date only; text not on the fetched page)
Fowler M. Scaling: Why Giants Don't Exist. University of Virginia lecture notes (teaching source)

geometric_similarity_mass_cubed.notes:
Quotes:
- Burton 2010 abstract: 'As he [Quetelet] realised, perfect isometry or geometric similarity requires that body mass varies with height cubed'.
- Burton 2018 full text: 'consider first a hypothetical set of individuals of different sizes but identical density and bodily proportions. Their masses must vary in proportion to both (sitting height)3 and height3 ... The BMIs of these isometric individuals would inevitably increase with height.'
- Haldane: 'These monsters were not only ten times as high as Christian, but ten times as wide and ten times as thick, so that their total weight was a thousand times his, or about eighty to ninety tons. Unfortunately the cross sections of their bones were only a hundred times those of Christian'.
- Fowler: 'its height, length and breadth will all be doubled, so its volume -- and hence its weight -- will increase eightfold'; and 'a giant flea is one hundred times larger in all dimensions, so its weight is up by a factor of a million. Its amount of muscle is also up by a factor of a million'.
Evidence quality: this is geometry, not a measurement, so the statement is exact for a true scaled copy. Burton 2010 and 2018 are peer-reviewed. Haldane is a classic popular essay. recommended_size_independent_index.notes:
Why this index:
- The height-cubed exponent is the only one that follows from geometry: constant for a scaled copy (Burton 2007, 2010, 2018; Haldane; Fowler).
- Allometric normalisation based on geometric similarity is the recommended practice when sizes differ (Jaric 2005).
- Weight/H^3 is an established index (Rohrer, tri-ponderal; Peterson 2017).
- The constant 1.8 m is Kouri's reference height, so S equals plain and Kouri-normalised FFMI at 1.80 m. That lets readers use the familiar FFMI landmarks (Schutz median 18.9, Kouri 25) on the S axis.
Where S stops being valid, or misleads:
1. Real tall men are not scaled copies. FFM goes roughly with H^1.86 to 2 (Heymsfield 2007), so S rates ordinary tall men lower and short men higher (ANSUR: about 12% between the tallest and shortest tenths). Kouri-normalised FFMI is the better human comparison between 1.55 and 2.05 m.
2. S is not a published FFM index (none found). Kouri's 25 is a sample maximum in normalised FFMI, which equals S only at 1.80 m. At other human heights the two differ by up to about 2.5 units.
3. S measures bulk for height (shape), not strength or physiology. It says nothing about whether a 3 m body of that shape could stand or move (Galileo, Haldane, Biewener).
4. S is very sensitive to the height used (3% per 1%) and to the assumed density and body fat.
5. Every S above the human data (about 40) is an extrapolation of geometry, not of any fitted human relation.

Correction (verifier): Keep S. Replace 'recommended practice' with 'one proposed approach (Jaric 2005)'. Cite Forbes/Wang 2012 as precedent for FFM proportional to H^3 across growth, and Burton 2007's endorsement of FFM/H^2 within adults as the counterpoint. Draw the landmarks as 'value at 1.80 m'. Present the meatball as a reference shape. Replace 'better' with 'closer to how real men's FFM scales with height (about H^2 to H^2.45)'.

verify.issue:
Choosing S = 1.8 x FFM / H^3 is defensible as a same-shape index, and the stated limits are mostly honest. Several supporting claims overstate the evidence:
(a) 'Allometric normalisation based on geometric similarity is the recommended practice (Jaric 2005)'. Jaric 2005 is a proposal, and Nevill fits exponents empirically, which for adult FFM against height gives about 2.
(b) Burton 2007 is cited for H^3, but its conclusion that BMI is valid in adults and 'properly divisible into fat mass and fat-free mass indices' (H^2) is left out.
(c) 'Not a published FFM index (none found)' misses Forbes's FFM = 10.3 x H^3 and Wang 2012's FFM = 10.8 x H^2.95 in males aged 5-59.
(d) The Schutz 18.9 and Kouri 25 landmarks are exact on the S axis only at 1.80 m; Kouri's boundary spans about S 24-27 over 1.60-1.95 m.
(e) The meatball is not an upper bound.
(f) 'Kouri-normalised FFMI is the better human comparison' is a judgement. Kouri's slope comes from 157 athletes of unknown height range, and Trexler 2017's slope was not significant.

kouri1995_fulltext_methods.label: Kouri et al. 1995, full text: sample, how non-use was checked, body-fat method, group values, and the 6.1 height slope

sources.title: Kouri EM, Pope HG Jr, Katz DL, Oliva P. Fat-free mass index in users and nonusers of anabolic-androgenic steroids. Clin J Sport Med 1995;5(4):223-228. Publisher's free full-text PDF (Ovid / Wolters Kluwer; scanned, 6 pages; read as page images)
Same article, publisher landing page reached from DOI 10.1097/00042752-199510000-00003 (marked 'Free', 'PDF Only')
Europe PMC record, PMID 7496846 (abstract)

kouri1995_fulltext_methods.notes:
Methods, p.223: 'One hundred fifty-six men in a large controlled study of athletes, recruited at gymnasiums in the Boston and Los Angeles areas, were administered physical examinations ... height, body weight, and body fat, the latter computed from the sum of six skinfold measurements using an equation derived from the data of Jackson and Pollock'. The equation is %fat = 0.217x1 - 0.00029x1^2 + 0.133x2 - 5.73, where x1 is the sum of the chest, thigh, ilium, abdomen, triceps and scapula skinfolds and x2 is age. One investigator (H.G.P.) took all the skinfolds.

Non-use, p.223-224: 'Each athlete's history of steroid use was obtained by detailed personal interview, supplemented by urine testing ... no evidence suggested that any athlete had deliberately misrepresented his steroid use, nor did any urine test contradict an athlete's verbal report.' p.226: 'all 74 nonusers produced urine samples negative for steroids.' A urine test shows only recent use, so past use rests on the interview.

Sample, p.224: 'complete skinfold measurements were not performed in 22 subjects, leaving 134 evaluable individuals'. Added to them were 23 men from a testosterone cypionate trial: 'five men who had formerly used anabolic steroids and 18 who had not'. On the non-users: 'The nonusers included many dedicated bodybuilders. Several had competed successfully in "natural" bodybuilding contests, two held world records in strength events, and many others were recognized by their associates as highly successful weightlifters.'

Formulas: FFM = weight x [1 - (%fat / 100)]; FFMI = FFM x height^-2.

Table 1 (mean +/- SD; the FFMI here is before height normalisation):
- Users: 1.79 +/- 0.075 m, 91.69 +/- 11.8 kg, 12.8 +/- 4.8% fat, FFMI 24.8 +/- 2.2.
- Non-users: 1.80 +/- 0.074 m, 82.06 +/- 13.0 kg, 12.5 +/- 5.5% fat, FFMI 21.8 +/- 1.8.

Users vs non-users, p.224: 'users extended well beyond the line, with 37 (45%) of the users attaining levels of FFMI beyond the uppermost of the nonusers.'

Height slope, p.224: 'we calculated the slope of a regression line drawn through a plot of all the "elite" nonuser athletes with FFMI scores of 22 or above ... This calculation yielded a slope of 6.1 kg/m3 ... Normalized FFMI = FFMI + 6.1 x (1.8 - h)'. The 1.8 m is 'the mean height of the nonusers'. The abstract's '6.3' does not appear in the body of the paper.

Height effect: the paper re-measured 'the shortest nonuser (height 1.59 m) and one of the tallest nonusers (height 1.93 m)'. Their unnormalised FFMIs were 23.5 and 25.4, yet 'the short athlete appeared more muscular'.

Limitations the authors give:
- 74 non-users 'might not have been large enough to exhibit fully the upper limits of muscularity naturally attainable'.
- The skinfold standard error is 3.4% fat. Their example: a 1.8 m, 90 kg man at 10% fat scores 25.0, and at 13% fat 24.2.
- 'it is possible that fat individuals might be able to exceed substantially an FFMI of 25 without steroids'. Only 6 non-users (8.1%) were above 20% fat.

Small internal slip: 'Fifty-two of the users (67% of the user group)'. 52/83 is 63%; 52/78 gym-study users is 67%.

Evidence quality: one cross-sectional sample of self-selected volunteers with one skinfold tester. It is strong evidence that these 74 men stopped below 25, and weak evidence for any population-wide ceiling.

Re-downloaded the publisher PDF. You need the Ovid cookie set by first loading the /fulltext/ page; a cold request is 307-redirected to HTML. The PDF's md5 matches the researcher's file. I read all 6 pages at 150-300 dpi and every number checks:
- n: 156 recruited, 134 evaluable, +23 from the testosterone trial (5 former users, 18 non-users). Totals 157 = 83 users + 74 non-users.
- Table 1: users 1.79±0.075 m, 91.69±11.8 kg, 12.8±4.8% fat, FFMI 24.8±2.2. Non-users 1.80±0.074 m, 82.06±13.0 kg, 12.5±5.5% fat, FFMI 21.8±1.8.

- 37 (45%) users beyond the top non-user. 'all 74 nonusers produced urine samples negative'. Six non-users (8.1%) above 20% fat. Skinfold SE 3.4%, with the 25.0 vs 24.2 example. The 1.59 m (23.5) and 1.93 m (25.4) men, and the 'appeared more muscular' quote. The '67%' slip (52/83 is 63%).

- Table 1 says only 'FFMI'. 'Before height normalisation' is an inference; it makes almost no difference at these mean heights.
- 18 of the 74 non-users came from a testosterone trial in 'normal men', not from gyms, so 'drug-free lifters' (used in the recommendations) overstates the group.

butt_frame_model_max_lbm.label: Casey Butt's frame-based prediction of maximum drug-free lean mass from height, wrist and ankle (self-published; not peer-reviewed)

sources.title: WeightTraining.nz, 'Casey Butt Calculator' (secondary; gives the imperial formula with 22.667/17.01 and the metric form with 322.4/241.9)
Fitmatic, 'Maximum Muscular Potential Calculator by Casey Butt' (secondary; constants 22.6670/17.0104, measuring sites, '~300 natural bodybuilding champions spanning from 1947 to 2010')
McDonald L. 'Four Models for Genetic Muscular Potential', BodyRecomposition, 2009, updated 2020 (Butt-calculator outputs table, image)
McDonald's Butt-model table image (5'8"/5'10"/6'0": 189/198/206 lb at 10% fat; LBM 170/178/185 lb)
Bony to Beastly, 'Natural Muscular Potential Calculator' (secondary; says it uses the 4th edition of Butt's book 'Your Muscular Potential')
Butt's original site (fetched; now redirects to a domain-parking service, router.parklogic.com)
ANSUR II Measurer's Handbook (Hotzman et al. 2011, NATICK/TR-11/017), sec. 6.4.5 Ankle Circumference and 6.4.93 Wrist Circumference
ANSUR II male CSV (repo copy at build-calculator/data/ansur2/; see builds.json ansur2_dataset)

butt_frame_model_max_lbm.notes:
The formula, as the two secondary calculators give it (the primary pages could not be reached): M = H^1.5 x (sqrt(W)/22.6670 + sqrt(A)/17.0104) x (F/224 + 1). M is maximum lean body mass in lb; H is height, W wrist and A ankle, all in inches; F is the body-fat % at which the mass is wanted. weighttraining.nz rounds the constants to 22.667 and 17.01, and gives a metric form (cm, kg) with 322.4 and 241.9.

Check: the formula reproduces to the pound the three outputs of Butt's own calculator that McDonald published (7 in wrist, 8.75 in ankle, 10% fat: LBM 170, 178 and 185 lb at 5'8", 5'10" and 6'0"). So the constants match Butt's calculator.

Measuring sites (fitmatic): wrist 'on the hand side of the styloid process'; ankle 'Smallest measurement just above your ankle'. ANSUR II measures the wrist at stylion with the upper edge of the tape 'just below the bony prominence at stylion', and the ankle as the 'Minimum horizontal circumference of the ankle'. So ANSUR frames are a fair input.

Data behind it:
- fitmatic (secondary): 'approximately 300 natural bodybuilding champions spanning from 1947 to 2010'.
- Butt's own sister article (reposted): 'a similar 6-year study I did on champion bodybuilders', based on 'drug-free champions both past and present'.
- McDonald: Butt 'has done an exhaustive analysis of top level natural bodybuilders'.
Drug-free status rests on the era (before about 1959) or federation testing. The measurements are contest and magazine figures.

Peer review and validation: none found. It was self-published on weightrainer.net and in the e-book 'Your Muscular Potential' (4th edition per bonytobeastly), with no journal paper, no published data set and no error statistics. fitmatic says results 'may deviate by up to approximately 3%' for unusual frames, without a source. McDonald quotes Butt's site: 'I haven't received any legitimate, verifiable statistics that significantly exceed the results of the equations'. Butt signs as Ph.D.; I did not verify the field.

weightrainer.net now redirects to a domain-parking service. The Wayback Machine (blocked by the egress policy) and archive.ph (connection reset) could not be reached from this sandbox.

Applied to ANSUR II men (my derivation):
- At 1.80 m with the median frame of the 1,814 men 175-185 cm tall (wrist 17.8 cm, ankle 23.2 cm): LBM 81.5 kg at 5% fat and 83.2 kg at 10%, which is FFMI (= S at 1.80 m) 25.1-25.7.
- Frames at the 5th to 95th percentile give 24.1-26.9.
- Applied to all 4,082 men at their own heights: plain FFMI median 25.3 at 5% fat and 25.8 at 10%; 5th-95th percentile 24.3-27.0.

The F/224 term makes 'lean' mass rise 2% between 5% and 10% fat. Mass scales as H^1.5 x frame, so the rescaled S of a Butt maximum falls with height: median S 29.7 at 155-160 cm, down to 23.8 at 190-195 cm (10% fat).

Evidence quality: low to moderate. It is a curve fitted to hand-picked champions, with unpublished data and no peer review, though its result sits close to Kouri's measured 25.

Formula and constants confirmed on weighttraining.nz (22.667, 17.01; metric 322.4, 241.9, which I re-derived exactly) and fitmatic (22.6670, 17.0104; 'approximately 300 natural bodybuilding champions spanning from 1947 to 2010'). McDonald's text confirms '7″ wrist and 8.75″ ankle'. His table gives 189/198/206 lb and LBM 170/178/185; I recompute 170.24, 177.80, 185.48. butt_max_girth_equations.label: Casey Butt's 'maximum muscular measurements' equations (chest, arm, forearm, neck, thigh, calf at about 10% fat): a per-body-part maximum, not one physique

sources.title: Butt C. 'Maximum Drug-Free Bodybuilding Potential, ed. 1.0' (The WeighTrainer), full-text repost on Canadian Brawn forum, 21 Nov 2018 (original site offline)

butt_max_girth_equations.notes:
Read as a full-text forum repost (header 'The WeighTrainer ... by Casey Butt, Ph.D.') because the original site is offline. Treat it as reported.

'Maximum Muscular Measurements (at approx. 10% body fat)', in inches:
- chest = 1.625W + 1.3682A + 0.3562H
- biceps = 1.1709W + 0.1350H
- forearms = 0.950W + 0.1041H
- neck = 1.1875W + 0.1301H
- thighs = 1.4737A + 0.1918H
- calves = 0.9812A + 0.1250H
W is the wrist 'measured on the hand side of the styloid process', A the ankle 'at the smallest point', H the height. Measuring sites: chest relaxed, tape under the armpits; biceps flexed at the largest point; forearm with the fist clenched, at the largest point; neck below the Adam's apple at the smallest point; thigh midway between hip and knee; calf at the largest point.

Author's caveats: 'The equations presented in this article outline a level of development beyond the capabilities of the vast majority of trainees, including most champions'; 'none of the listed champions attained all of the predictions in each of their body parts'. Each equation is a fit to the most extreme champions for that one body part (for example, the chest is set by Reg Park). So a figure with all six maxima would exceed any single natural champion.

His observations: 'the largest lean arms I know of ... are/were 2.53 times wrist circumference ... 0.27 times height'. His probability claim (95% of a million trainees could not beat these by even 1%) assumes the champions are the best of a random sample of known size, which he does not show.

At 1.80 m with the ANSUR median frame of men 175-185 cm tall (my calculation): chest 124.8 cm, biceps 45.1, forearm 35.6, neck 44.6, thigh 68.7, calf 45.3. The repost's worked example mixes ankle values: it states 9.25 in, uses 9.25 for chest and thigh, but 9.0 for the calf.

Evidence quality: low (self-published, fitted to selected maxima). It is usable only as a labelled 'prediction' for a natural-limit silhouette's girths.

berkhan_height_minus_100.label: Martin Berkhan's rule: height in cm minus 100 = stage weight in kg at 5-6% fat (a coach's rule from about four men)

berkhan_height_minus_100.notes:
Berkhan: '(Height in centimeters - 100) = Body weight in kilo ("shredded", i.e. 5-6% body fat). Example: If your height is 180 cm (5'11), subtract 100 and you get 80. 80 kg (176 lbs) is your maximum muscular potential when you are in peak condition'. His basis: 'a formula based on the heights and body weights of natural bodybuilders on competition day' and 'I've only known a handful of guys who I was 100% sure of being natural. His data points, with body fat 'estimated':
- Marcus: 181 cm, 79 kg, 4-4.5%.
- Andreaz: 169 cm, 69-71 kg, 5-6%.
- Robert: 182 cm, 82 kg, 7%.
- Himself: 186 cm, 87.5 kg; '186 cm/86 kg (-100) on competition day (5.5% body fat)'. He has not competed.

Limits he states: 'most accurate for men in the 170-190 cm height range'. Offsets by height: 190 cm, -101; 180 cm, -100; 170 cm, -99; 160 cm, -98. 'the true limit will not differ from height - 100 in any meaningful way'. He reports 'a 2% drop in body weight' on stage day.

McDonald's Berkhan table has a 'Lean Body Mass' column of 170/178/185 lb, which looks copied from the Butt column. At 5% fat, Berkhan's 160/171/182 lb are 152/162/173 lb of lean mass.

The journal is Am J Hum Biol 6(5):613-618, not J Am Coll Nutr as the task named it; Europe PMC and the DOI agree. I read the abstract only (Wiley paywall; Semantic Scholar lists no open copy).

Abstract: '37 professional Japanese Sumo wrestlers, 14 highly trained bodybuilders, and 26 untrained men were investigated for body composition (fat mass and FFM) and cross-sectional areas (CSA) of limb muscles, by hydrodensitometry and ultrasound'. 'Six of the wrestlers had more than 100 kg of FFM, including the largest one of 121.3 kg (stature: 186 cm, mass: 181 kg, %fat: 33.0%). The FFM/stature ratio of elite Sumo wrestlers averaged at 0.61 kg/cm, with the highest 0.66 kg/cm. It is suggested that a FFM/stature ratio of 0.7 kg/cm may be an upper limit in humans.' Drug testing is not mentioned.

My conversions for the largest wrestler: FFMI 121.3/1.86^2 = 35.1; S = 1.8 x 121.3/1.86^3 = 33.9; Kouri-normalised 34.7. A limit per cm of height converts to FFMI only at a stated height: 0.7 kg/cm at 1.80 m is 126 kg of FFM, FFMI 38.9 = S 38.9 (S 41.1 at 1.75 m, 36.8 at 1.85 m).

- Two-compartment densitometry assumes one FFM density. At 33% fat, much of the 'fat-free' mass is organ, water and the fat-free part of adipose tissue, not muscle. - Kanehisa 1998 (23 professionals) reported FFM from 59.1 to 107.6 kg.

natural_limit_anchor_conversions.label: Natural-limit anchors converted to the rescaled index S = 1.8*FFM/H^3, with the conversion rules

sources.title: Kouri et al. 1995 full text (k = 6.1; reference height 1.8 m)
Trexler et al. 2017 full text (k = 2.943)
Todd 2008 (heights used for the Mr America conversion)
Chappell, Simper & Helms 2019, Table 1 (builds.json chappell2019_natural_pro_bodybuilders)

natural_limit_anchor_conversions.notes:
Rules:
- Plain FFMI F = FFM/H^2. S = 1.8*FFM/H^3 = 1.8F/H.
- A height-normalised index N = F + k(1.8 - H), with k = 6.1 (Kouri) or 2.943 (Trexler).
- At exactly H = 1.80 m, F = N = S. A value 'normalised to 1.8 m' is therefore already on the chart's basis for a 1.80 m man.
- For a real person at another height: F = N - k(1.8 - H), then S = 1.8F/H.
- A sample statistic (mean, percentile, maximum) without individual heights can be converted only roughly, at the sample's mean height; I flag those as approximate.
Scripts: scratchpad scripts/anchor_conversions.py, kouri_t2_S.py, todd_table.py, frame_models.py, butt_ansur.py.

Scaling mismatch: S assumes FFM grows as H^3 (same shape). Kouri's elite non-users implied about H^2.44, and Butt's formula about H^1.5 x frame. So on S, short naturals score higher and tall ones lower. Kouri's 1.59 m non-user (FFMI 23.5) is S 26.6, while his 1.93 m non-user (25.4) is S 23.7. The Kouri 25 line runs from S 26.3 at 1.65 m to 23.9 at 1.95 m.

Items from existing keys:
- Chappell 2019 PROs: 1.77 m, 82.3 kg end of prep (self-reported), 5% fat assumed; FFMI 25.0, S 25.4.
- Rossow 2013: FFMI 24.9, height unknown, so S is 24.9 only if 1.80 m (23.6 at 1.90 m, 26.4 at 1.70 m).
- Kouri's modern bodybuilders: S given at the 1.80 m basis from the normalised values; heights not printed.

ansur2_outline_landmark_definitions.label: ANSUR II landmark heights for the outline: what each marks, and the standing posture

sources.title: Hotzman J et al. 2011, Measurer's Handbook: US Army and Marine Corps Anthropometric Surveys 2010-2011, NATICK/TR-11/017 (PDF)
Gordon CC et al. 2014, 2012 Anthropometric Survey of U.S. Army Personnel: Methods and Summary Statistics, NATICK/TR-15/007 (PDF)

ansur2_outline_landmark_definitions.notes:
Fetched both PDFs and extracted the text with pdftotext.

Standing posture (6.1.1): "stand erect, with their weight evenly distributed on both feet, heels together as much as possible, legs and trunk straight without stiffness ... The arms are to hang relaxed with the elbows lightly touching the sides with the palms of the hands beside, but not touching, the thighs. On individuals with muscular upper arms, the elbows may not touch the sides." Most heights are taken "at the maximum point of quiet respiration".

Landmark definitions:
- Stature: "The vertical distance from a standing surface to the top of the head", head in the Frankfurt plane, hair compressed.
- Cervicale: "The most prominent palpable point of the spine of the seventh cervical vertebra". ANSUR 1988 used the 'superior palpable point'.
- Suprasternale: "The inferior point of the jugular notch of the sternum".
- Acromion: "The point of intersection of the lateral border of the acromial process and a line running down the middle of the shoulder from the neck to the tip of the shoulder."
- Axilla height: "the right axillary fold, as designated by the anterior scye on the torso landmark". That mark is drawn at the top of a level rule clamped in the armpit.
- Chest height: to chest point anterior, "The most anterior right point on the chest". ANSUR 1988 used the nipple (thelion) for men.
- Waist height: to "the center of the navel" (omphalion), abdomen not tensed.
- Buttock height: "the level of the maximum protrusion of the right buttock".
- Trochanterion: "The superior point of the greater trochanter of the right femur of a standing participant". The handbook warns it "can be a difficult landmark to locate".
- Crotch height: the blade is raised into firm contact with the crotch, and "The computer will add 1 cm to the recorded dimension to account for the width of the anthropometer blade."
- Knee height, midpatella: "The anterior point halfway between the top and bottom of the patella", with the knee relaxed.
- Lateral malleolus: "The most lateral point of the right lateral malleolus".
- Wrist height: to stylion ("The inferior point of the bottom of the radius"), with "the arms ... extended downwards with the elbow, wrist, and fingers held rigidly straight. The arms lightly touch the sides. The palms face inward (medially)."

All landmarks are on the right side. Every height is a vertical distance from the floor in this standing posture, so an outline drawn from them is a relaxed, arms-down stance, not an A-pose.

I re-downloaded TR-11/017 (sha matches the published file size, 5,224,258 bytes) and checked every quoted definition: standing posture 6.1.1, stature, cervicale with the ANSUR 1988 'superior palpable point' footnote, suprasternale, acromion, axilla/anterior scye, chest point, omphalion, buttock, trochanterion and its 'difficult landmark' caution, crotch +1 cm, midpatella, lateral malleolus, stylion and wrist height. All quotes match. I checked all 22 printed page numbers by script and all match (73, 152, 27, 153, 23, 78, 82, 56, 28, 103, 70, 167, 95, 69, 104, 48, 133, 44, 136, 60, 170, 159).

Two omissions:
- Not every height uses the 6.1.1 posture. Tibial and lateral femoral epicondyle heights are taken with the feet together on a table, and wrist height with the arms 'rigidly straight'.
- The handbook warns that tibiale (p.65) and the lateral femoral epicondyle (p.43) are 'difficult or impossible to locate accurately in heavily muscled participants'. That matters for a chart that extends to bodybuilders.

ansur2_outline_breadth_depth_definitions.label: ANSUR II trunk, head, hand and foot breadths and depths: exact definitions (incl. whether chest breadth includes the lats)

values.chest_breadth_state: full inspiration, tissue compressed to rib cage

sources.title: Hotzman J et al. 2011, NATICK/TR-11/017 Measurer's Handbook (PDF)
Gordon CC et al. 2014, NATICK/TR-15/007 (PDF)

ansur2_outline_breadth_depth_definitions.notes:
Chest breadth (6.4.24): "The maximum horizontal breadth of the chest at the level of the chest point anterior landmark." The participant puts both hands on the hips and takes a deep breath. The measurer is told to "Compress the tissue firmly to ensure contact with the rib cage, ask the participant to lower the arms, and take the measurement. The measurement is taken at maximum inspiration". Breast tissue is excluded. TR-15/007 footnote: "This measurement also differs from ANSUR because the tissue is now compressed and the measurement is taken at maximum inspiration."

The latissimus is never mentioned. Lat tissue at that level is squeezed against the ribs by the caliper, not excluded by rule. So chest breadth is a compressed rib-cage width, not the outline width of the torso.

Other trunk measures:
- Chest depth: from chest point anterior to the back at the same level, at quiet respiration, "only enough pressure to maintain contact".
- Chest girth: taken at quiet respiration. "The tape will span body hollows in this measurement."
- Waist breadth: at omphalion. "Care must be taken not to compress the soft tissue."
- Waist depth: from waist omphalion anterior to posterior, right hand on the chest, abdomen not tensed.
- Hip breadth: "The horizontal distance between the lateral buttock landmarks on the sides of the hips", standing with the arms slightly away from the body. It sits at the buttock-protrusion level, the same level as buttock depth and buttock girth, so it is not necessarily the widest hip level.
- Buttock depth: "The horizontal depth of the torso at the level of the maximum protrusion of the right buttock", from the posterior buttock point to the abdomen.

Head, hand and foot:
- Head breadth: "The maximum horizontal breadth of the head above the ears" (euryon).
- Head length: glabella to opisthocranion, at its maximum, hair compressed.
- Hand breadth: "between the landmarks at metacarpale II and metacarpale V", so the thumb is excluded.
- Hand length: stylion to the tip of the middle finger.
- Foot length: pternion to the tip of the longest toe, on a Brannock device, standing.
- Foot breadth: "The maximum breadth of the right foot", at the metatarsophalangeal level, standing.

verify.issue:
Every quote is verified in TR-11/017: chest breadth (p.100; compress 'firmly to ensure contact with the rib cage', taken at maximum inspiration), chest circumference (p.101; 'The tape will span body hollows'), chest depth (p.102), hip breadth (p.127), buttock depth (p.94), waist breadth (p.163; 'Care must be taken not to compress'), head breadth and length, hand and foot. The TR-15/007 chest-breadth footnote is verified on p.89. The word 'latissimus' or 'lat' never appears in either report (grep).

'A compressed rib-cage width, not the outline width' is the researcher's inference from the procedure, not a handbook statement. It is reasonable, but it should be worded as an inference.
verify.corrected: Reword to: 'By the procedure (firm compression to the rib cage), chest breadth is narrower than the visible torso outline (our inference; the handbook does not say so).'

ansur2_biacromial_vs_bideltoid.label: Biacromial vs bideltoid breadth in ANSUR II: bone-to-bone vs widest muscle across the arms

values.orig_mm: biacromial p50 415, bideltoid p50 509; half-differences p50 47 mm and 110 mm

sources.title: Hotzman J et al. 2011, NATICK/TR-11/017 (sections 6.4.9 and 6.4.12)
Gordon CC et al. 2014, NATICK/TR-15/007 (dimensions 8 and 11)
ANSUR II male CSV (OPEN Design Lab), local copy sha256 0547aea0170e5293...

ansur2_biacromial_vs_bideltoid.notes:
Biacromial breadth: "The distance between the right and left acromion landmarks on the tips of the shoulder." It is taken in anthropometric sitting with a beam caliper from behind, "Use sufficient pressure to maintain firm contact with the skin". It is a bony width.

Bideltoid breadth: "The maximum horizontal distance between the lateral margins of the upper arms on the deltoid muscles." The caliper blades are brushed up and down the arms, "When the blades lightly touch the skin on both sides, withdraw the instrument". The handbook adds "the deltoid landmarks are NOT used for this dimension" and "This measurement should never be taken lower than the bottom of the deltoid muscles."

TR-15/007 says both are seated: "The shoulders and upper arms are relaxed, and the forearms and hands are extended forward horizontally with the palms facing each other". Both are at quiet respiration. Bideltoid therefore includes the soft tissue of both arms; it is the widest front-view width across the shoulders with the arms down.

The numbers in values are my arithmetic on the 4,082 men (script ansur_outline.py): (bideltoid - biacromial)/2, (bideltoid - chest breadth)/2, and bideltoid / shoulder circumference. Shoulder circumference is taken at the deltoid points. Caveat: both breadths are seated while acromial height is standing.

ansur2_joint_centre_heights_estimate.label: Joint-centre heights for the ANSUR II template, from de Leva's offsets (shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee)

sources.title: ANSUR II male CSV (OPEN Design Lab)
de Leva P 1996, J Biomech 29:1223 (Table 2 offsets)

ansur2_joint_centre_heights_estimate.notes:
Script ansur_outline.py, section 'joint_centre_heights_deLeva_offsets'. Rules applied to each man:
- Shoulder = acromial height - 0.104 x acromion-radiale.
- Elbow = acromial height - acromion-radiale + 0.0431 x acromion-radiale. Radiale height is not in ANSUR II, so it is approximated with the arm hanging.
- Wrist = wrist height - 0.006 x radiale-stylion.
- Hip = trochanterion + 0.0071 x (trochanterion - tibiale).
- Knee = tibiale + 0.0739 x (trochanterion - tibiale).

ANSUR's acromion (border of the acromial process meeting the mid-shoulder line) is close to de Leva's ("most lateral point on the lateral margin of the acromial process"). ANSUR's median acromion-radiale of 335 mm is close to de Leva's 331.8 mm.

The knee centre lands 8 mm (median) above the ANSUR lateral femoral epicondyle, so epicondyle height is a usable proxy. Shoulder longitudinal offsets are treated as vertical, which holds only with the arm hanging.

This is an estimate built from a 6-cadaver source applied to 4,082 soldiers.

Correction (verifier): Set the status to 'estimate'. Add the heavily-muscled landmark caution, and the 'knee pivot point' wording as support for using epicondyle height as the knee centre.

hip_joint_centre_vs_greater_trochanter.label: Hip joint centre height is about level with the top of the greater trochanter (within about 1 cm)

sources.title: Hu H et al. Intraoperative method of femoral head central measurement to prevent leg length discrepancy following hemiarthroplasty. Front Surg 2022;9:1055199 (full text via Europe PMC)
de Leva P 1996, J Biomech 29:1223 (Table 2: hip +3.2 mm vs trochanterion)

hip_joint_centre_vs_greater_trochanter.notes:
Hu 2022, Table 3: "the median number of VD-CFH-TGTAAF ... on the nonoperative side were 6.35 mm (IQR, 4.33–9.75 mm)". VD-CFH-TGTAAF is the vertical distance from the centre of the femoral head to the tip of the greater trochanter, along the femoral anatomical axis, on radiographs.

The paper does not state the direction of this distance. De Leva places the HJC slightly proximal (3.2 mm) to trochanterion.

Caveats: elderly femoral-neck-fracture patients (sex mix not checked), the uninjured side, n = 33. The skin landmark trochanterion is palpated, and the handbook calls it difficult to locate. Treat this as 'level with trochanterion, within about 1 cm'.

verify.issue:
Hu 2022 Table 3 is verified: 6.35 mm (IQR 4.33–9.75) and femoral offset 49.20 mm (46.50–52.70), on the non-operative side; the distance is measured along the femoral anatomical axis on radiographs. The direction is not stated, as the researcher says.

The sex mix the researcher left unchecked is in Table 1: the 33-patient group was 8 men and 25 women, median age 81 (78–82.5), femoral-neck-fracture patients at one Fujian hospital. Applied to young men this is weak evidence. The headline rests mainly on de Leva's 3.2 mm.
verify.corrected: Fill in: 'IM-CMFH group 8 men / 25 women, median age 81; radiographic bony trochanter tip, not the skin landmark.' Keep the claim at 'level with trochanterion within about 1 cm', resting mainly on de Leva.

inter_hip_joint_centre_distance_estimate.label: Distance between the two hip joint centres: about 0.10 of stature, about half the ANSUR hip breadth

sources.title: Hara R et al. 2016, Sci Rep 6:37707 (y equations)
de Leva P 1996, J Biomech 29:1223 (Table 3: bispinous breadth 255.7 mm scaled, from Clauser 1969 cadavers)

inter_hip_joint_centre_distance_estimate.notes:
My arithmetic, not a measured value.
- Route 1: 2 x (10 + 0.329 x IA), with IA = 255.7 mm, gives 188 mm. IA is the scaled male bispinous breadth in de Leva Table 3, from Clauser et al. 1969's 13 male cadavers, mean age 49. 188 mm is 0.108 of de Leva's 1.741 m stature.
- Route 2: 2 x (8 + 0.086 x LL), with an assumed LL of 0.89 m (ASIS to medial malleolus for a 1.755 m man; ANSUR II has no iliospinale height), gives 169 mm, or 0.096 of 1.755 m.

Both estimates are about half of ANSUR median hip breadth (344 mm). Use it only to place the leg pivots for the silhouette and for the 'thighs touch' limit, labelled estimate.

verify.issue:
The arithmetic checks: 2 × (10 + 0.329 × 255.7) = 188.3 mm; 2 × (8 + 0.086 × 890) = 169.1 mm; 0.108 and 0.096 of stature; 0.49–0.55 of hip breadth. De Leva Table 3 is confirmed: bispinous breadth 29.40% (N = 1), scaled to 255.7 mm, from Clauser 1969 (13 male cadavers, mean age 49).

Caveat: the IA equation pools children. Hara's age-group IA model, y = 34 + 0.151 IA + 16.714 × age, gives about 179 mm for an adult if the dummy is coded 0/1. That coding is not stated, so it is unverified. 179 mm is still inside the 169–188 mm range. The 'estimate' status is right.
verify.corrected: Add a note: 'Hara's IA equation is fitted on pooled children and adults; the adult-intercept variant gives about 179 mm (dummy coding assumed), within the range.'

glenohumeral_centre_estimation_methods.label: Shoulder (glenohumeral) joint centre: published estimation methods and their accuracy

sources.title: Meskers CG et al. In vivo estimation of the glenohumeral joint rotation center from scapular bony landmarks by linear regression. J Biomech 1998;31:93-96 (abstract, Europe PMC)
Campbell AC et al. MRI development and validation of two new predictive methods of glenohumeral joint centre location identification. J Biomech 2009;42:1527-1532 (abstract, Europe PMC)
Vicon FAQ: required subject measurements for Plug-in Gait (shoulder offset)
Tsai CY et al. 2012, Biomed Eng Online 11:87 (describes Rab 2002 constant-offset method; full text)
Rab G, Petuskey K, Bagley A. A method for determination of upper extremity kinematics. Gait Posture 2002;15:113-119 (abstract, Europe PMC)

glenohumeral_centre_estimation_methods.notes:
Meskers 1998 abstract: regression on 36 cadaver specimens predicted the rotation centre with RMSE 2.32, 2.69 and 3.04 mm. It needs scapular landmarks, which a silhouette lacks.

Campbell 2009 abstract: 20 subjects with MRI. Their new regression gave "an GHJ location error of 13+/-2 mm"; six established methods were all worse.

Vicon FAQ: shoulder offset is "The vertical distance from the center of the glenohumeral joint to the marker on the acromion clavicular joint", and "Some researchers have used the (anterior/posterior girth)/2". That is an industry rule of thumb, not data.

Tsai 2012 describes Rab 2002 as "a constant offset method which estimates the rotation center using constant distance ratio relative to acromion marker and the mid-point between lateral and medial epicondyle markers". The ratio itself was not verified; Rab's full text is paywalled and his abstract does not give it.

The only usable surface-landmark number fetched is de Leva's 34.5 mm below the acromion (see deleva1996_joint_centre_offsets). Expect errors of about 1-2 cm.

verify.issue:
All abstracts are re-fetched and match:
- Meskers: 36 cadaver scapula and humerus sets; RMSE 2.32, 2.69, 3.04 mm
- Campbell: 20 subjects; '13+/-2 mm' location error; inter-tester 6 ± 4 mm; better than the six established methods
- Rab abstract: no ratio
- Tsai 2012: the constant-offset quote is exact
The Vicon FAQ quotes are exact. Its offset is measured to the acromio-clavicular joint marker, not the lateral acromion tip, so it is not directly comparable to de Leva's 34.5 mm. 'Reported' is the right status.

head_height_fraction_male.label: Head height (crown to chin) as a fraction of stature: about 0.13 to 0.14 (central about 0.133, 7.2 to 7.8 heads); depends on the measuring instrument

sources.title: AIST Anthropometric Database 1991-92, item A36 total head height
AIST 1991-92 item A33 tragion to vertex height
AIST 1991-92 item B1 stature
ANSUR II male CSV (tragion-top of head, stature, cervicale)

head_height_fraction_male.notes:
ANSUR II has no crown-to-chin measure; only tragion-top of head, 131 mm. AIST A36 definition (translated): distance from the menton/gnathion point to the plane touching the top of the head, perpendicular to the Frankfurt plane. Seated, with a head gauge.

The ANSUR-scaled value multiplies each soldier's tragion-top by the AIST ratio 238.7/138.6 (script ansur_outline.py, 'head_height_estimate'). That ratio comes from Japanese men, whose tragion-top/stature (0.081) is larger than ANSUR's (0.075). Population and instrument differences both play a part.

Range: about 7.2-7.8 heads per stature (0.13-0.14 of stature). The chin sits about 13 mm above cervicale height in the ANSUR estimate.

Correction (verifier): Status: 'estimate' for the ANSUR-scaled values; AIST's 0.139 is 'measured', for Japanese men. Report head height as 0.13–0.14 of stature (7.2–7.8 heads), with a central value of about 0.133. Note that the ANSUR scaling depends on instrument: 0.129 with AIST's ratio, 0.133 with Hoshi's caliper-consistent ratio. Do not headline '7.8 heads'.

The AIST images re-read correctly: A36 238.7 (SD 8.03, n 217), from gnathion to the vertex plane, perpendicular to the Frankfurt plane, seated, head gauge plus height gauge; A33 138.6 (5.98); B1 1714.0 (62.55). Problems:
1. Status. The ANSUR-scaled half is a cross-population, cross-instrument estimate, not 'derived' data.
2. Bias the notes understate. The A33 image shows AIST's tragion-vertex is significantly larger (**) than comparison surveys measured with a rod caliper: Hoshi 132.1 (also Japanese) and USAF 129.7. A gap that large within Japanese samples points to method more than population.
   - ANSUR's tragion-top is a caliper measurement (131 mm), so dividing by AIST's 138.6 likely biases the ANSUR head height low.
   - Hoshi's own pair (A36 234.6 / A33 132.1 = 1.776) applied to ANSUR gives 0.133 of stature (7.5 heads), not 0.129 (7.8).

hand_foot_head_silhouette_fractions_male.label: Hand, foot and head proportions for silhouettes (fractions of stature)

sources.title: ANSUR II male CSV (OPEN Design Lab)
AIST 1991-92 item L16 hand thickness
AIST 1991-92 item M6 dorsal arch height

hand_foot_head_silhouette_fractions_male.notes:
ANSUR fractions come from ansur_outline.py. Hand breadth is metacarpale II-V, without the thumb. Fingertip height = wrist height - hand length, as in TR-15/007 D12; arms straight, palms in.

AIST items:
- L16 hand thickness: maximum thickness at the head of the 3rd metacarpal, 27.5 mm (SD 2.65, n 214).
- M6 dorsal arch height: floor to the cuneiform point, 61.9 mm (SD 5.43, n 214).
- D3 maximum body breadth: across the arms at the lateral humeral epicondyle level, arms hanging, 469.9 mm.
These are fractions of AIST mean stature (1.714 m), Japanese men.

In an A-pose with palms facing in, the front view shows the hand's thickness (about 0.016 of stature) and the side view its breadth (about 0.050). The front view of a foot shows breadth and instep height. The side view shows length and the ankle at about 0.04 of stature.

ellipse_volume_model_accuracy_recheck.label: Published accuracy of elliptical-zone and geometric volume models (re-check of existing keys)

sources.title: Chiu CY et al. Validation of body volume acquisition by using elliptical zone method. Int J Sports Med 2016;37:1117-1123 (abstract, Europe PMC)
Williams G et al. Accuracy of body mass prediction using segmental inertia parameters modelled from photographic images. ISBS Proceedings 2013 (PDF, Table 1)
Jensen RK 1978, J Biomech 11:349-358 (record only, no abstract)

ellipse_volume_model_accuracy_recheck.notes:
This relies on the existing keys ezone_volume_accuracy and inertia_model_mass_accuracy_table; I re-fetched both sources and the numbers hold.

Chiu 2016: "The relative technical error of measurement (TEM) of total body volume estimations was around 3% for E-Zone". Upper torso, lower torso, thigh, shank, upper arm and lower arm were "accurately (relative TEM<10%)"; neck, hand and foot were poor.

Williams 2013 Table 1 (secondary): "Jensen (1978) Photo 408 ... <2", "Yeadon (1990) Direct 95 ... < 2.1", "Gittoes et al. (2009) Photo 95 ... < 2.9", "Hatze (1980) Direct 242 ... < 0.05". The column is "% accuracy of predicted body mass".

Jensen's original is not accessible. Important: elliptical-zone models are accurate for volume (area integrated along the body), even though a single trunk ellipse from caliper breadths misses the chest girth by about 24% (ansur2_ellipse_vs_girth_male). Volume and girth accuracy are different questions.

Correction (verifier): Status: 'reported' (Williams secondary table). Keep Chiu as 'measured' (abstract only). Hatze: '<0.05 as printed in a column headed %; suspect'.

meatball_and_other_shapes.label: The meatball and two bigger shapes, on the score
meatball_and_other_shapes.notes: Score of a solid shape as tall as the figure: 1.8 x density x (volume / H^3) x (1 - fat). A ball of diameter H holds pi/6 H^3; a cylinder as wide as it is tall pi/4 H^3; a cube H^3. The meatball is where the owner chose to end the scale; a body wider than it is tall could hold more.
